skill_title: Apply Coulomb's Law to calculate force between point charges
notes: 20 items: 11 lifted, 9 fresh. Coulomb's Law definition + force between two point charges; signs; inverse-square law; sharing charge through contact.

items.question: State COULOMB'S LAW in words.
items.expectedAnswer: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force acts along the line joining the two charges.
items.explanation: Three marks: 'product of charges' + 'inversely proportional to r²' + 'along line joining charges'. F = kQ₁Q₂/r².

items.question: Two point charges Q and 2Q are separated by distance r. The electrostatic force between them is F. If the distance is DOUBLED, the new force is:
items.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r ⇒ 1/r² × ¼ ⇒ F becomes F/4.

items.question: Sphere X has charge +2q and sphere Y has charge −6q. They are brought into contact and then separated. The original force between them was F. What is the new force after contact?
items.explanation: Originally |F| ∝ |2q × 6q| = 12q². After contact (identical spheres): total charge −4q shared equally ⇒ −2q each. |F'| ∝ |2q × 2q| = 4q². Ratio = 4/12 = 1/3 (magnitude). So new force = F/3 (now repulsive, both negative).

items.question: Sphere R has charge +5 × 10⁻⁹ C and sphere S has charge −6 × 10⁻⁹ C. The electrostatic force between them is 1.2 × 10⁻³ N (attractive). Calculate the distance r between R and S. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Charges X (−7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) and Y (+7.2 × 10⁻⁹ C) are placed 0.03 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Two small charged spheres A (+4 μC) and B (−6 μC) are placed 0.03 m apart in air. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between Q₁ = +4 × 10⁻⁶ C and Q₂ = −6 × 10⁻⁶ C placed 0.3 m apart. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)
Q₁ = +5 × 10⁻⁶ C and Q₂ = +5 × 10⁻⁶ C are placed 0.4 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. (k = 9 × 10⁹.)
items.explanation: Same-sign charges repel. F ≈ 1.41 N along the line joining the charges, directed outward from each.

items.question: Two opposite charges (one positive, one negative) are released from rest and move towards each other under their mutual attraction. Which statement best describes the ACCELERATION of each charge as they approach?
items.explanation: F = kq₁q₂/r². As they approach, r decreases ⇒ F increases ⇒ a = F/m increases. (Both charges accelerate more rapidly the closer they get.)

items.question: Two charges 5 nC and −2 nC are 0.10 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻².)

Two identical metal spheres carry equal positive charges of +6 μC each. The force between them is 4 N. They are then touched together (so they share charge equally) and returned to the same positions. What is the new force between them?
items.explanation: Touching identical spheres shares total charge equally — each still ends up with +6 μC (because they already had equal charges). So the force is unchanged: 4 N.

items.question: Two metal spheres carry charges of +8 μC and +2 μC and the force between them is F. They are briefly touched together and returned to their positions. What is the new force in terms of F?
items.explanation: Original: F ∝ 8 × 2 = 16. After contact: each sphere has (8+2)/2 = +5 μC. New ∝ 5 × 5 = 25. Ratio = 25/16. F' = (25/16)F.

items.question: A learner says: 'Coulomb's force can have a negative magnitude.' Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: No. Force MAGNITUDE is always positive. The negative sign in F = kQ₁Q₂/r² when one charge is negative just tells us the force is ATTRACTIVE (not 'pointing in the negative direction'). When reporting magnitudes, take the absolute value of the charges in the formula.
items.explanation: The sign of Coulomb's force tells you attraction (negative product) or repulsion (positive product), not direction. Magnitude is a positive scalar.

items.question: Calculate how many electrons must be removed from a neutral sphere to give it a charge of +1.6 nC. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
items.explanation: n = Q/e = 1.6 × 10⁻⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 10¹⁰ = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ electrons removed.

items.question: Two point charges experience a force of 10 N when 1 m apart. What is the force when they are moved to 0.5 m apart?
items.explanation: F ∝ 1/r². Halving r ⇒ F × 4. New F = 40 N.

items.question: Two point charges experience a force of 24 N. If one of the charges is TRIPLED while the distance is kept the same, what is the new force?
items.explanation: F ∝ Q₁ × Q₂. Tripling one charge triples F. New F = 72 N.

items.question: An electron and a proton are separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them. (k = 9 × 10⁹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
What is the SI unit of charge?
items.explanation: 1 C = charge transported by 1 A for 1 s.

items.question: Two point charges Q and Q each repel one another with a force of 100 N. If both charges are HALVED and the distance between them is HALVED, what is the new force?
items.explanation: F ∝ Q₁Q₂/r². Halve each Q ⇒ multiply by ¼. Halve r ⇒ multiply by 4. Net change: ¼ × 4 = 1. Force unchanged at 100 N.

items.question: Which TWO requirements does Coulomb's Law strictly assume about the charged objects?
items.expectedAnswer: (1) The charges must be POINT CHARGES (or behave as such — small spheres at large separations approximate this). (2) The charges must be at REST relative to each other (or moving slowly enough that magnetic effects are negligible). Also: the medium is usually assumed to be vacuum/air.
items.explanation: Point charges + at rest + uniform medium. For spheres, the centre-to-centre distance is used.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_LAW_STATEMENT: Coulomb's Law statement missing 'product', 'inversely proportional to r²', or 'along line'
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_INVERSE_SQUARE_LAW: Misapplies inverse-square scaling (e.g. halves F when r doubles)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_CHARGE_SHARING: Doesn't equally share charge between identical spheres in contact
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_MAGNITUDE_ONLY: Treats signed Coulomb force as a magnitude (or vice versa)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_REARRANGE: Algebra mistake when solving F = kQ₁Q₂/r² for r or Q
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_R_SQUARED: Forgets to square r in denominator
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_RATIO: Wrong scaling when changing Q and r simultaneously
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_CHARGE_QUANTIZED: Forgets Q = n·e for counting electrons
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COULOMB_ASSUMPTIONS: Can't state the point-charge / at-rest assumptions
